citation.title: Does Regression Produce Representative Estimates of Causal Effects?

standing_assumptions:
The work is Aronow and Samii, ‘Does Regression Produce Representative Estimates of Causal Effects?’, American Journal of Political Science 60(1): 250–267 (2016). Printed p. 249 + N is PDF p. N; Appendices A, B and C are printed pp. 262–265 (PDF pp. 13–16). Every passage below was read from the page images. The official erratum (AJPS 61(2): 504, 2017) concerns printed pp. 258 and 260 only and touches no target.

[Sampling and data: section ‘Data, Potential Outcomes, and Causal Effects’, p. 252 (PDF p. 3)] “Suppose that we begin with a population of interest and draw a sample indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, n$. We assume that the sample is self-weighting and representative—each member of the population has an equal probability of being selected. … All of the results in this article continue to apply if we substitute sampling from a fixed population with the super-population assumption. For all $i$ that appear in the sample, we measure (a) a causal factor of interest, or “treatment,” $D_i$, which may be continuous or binary; (b) a $K$-length row vector of control variables, $X_i$, that exhibit no perfect colinearities or measurement error; and (c) an outcome, $Y_i$. The sampling or super-population assumption implies that $D_i$, $X_i$, and $Y_i$ are random variables, although not necessarily independent.”

[Potential outcomes: p. 252 (PDF p. 3)] “for every potential value of $D_i$, each unit $i$ is assumed to possess a well-defined response. Thus, if $D_i$ can take on the values $d_1, d_2, \ldots$, then unit $i$’s potential outcomes are given by the corresponding values $Y_i(d_1), Y_i(d_2), \ldots$.”

[Expression (1): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “we suppose that potential outcomes take the following form: $Y_i(d) = Y_i(0) + \tau_i \cdot d$, (1) where $\tau_i$ is the causal effect for unit $i$ and $d$ is an arbitrary value of $D_i$. When the treatment is binary, $D_i \in \{0, 1\}$, then this characterization is completely general.”

[Expression (2): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “we assume that the control variables in $X_i$ are indeed sufficient for removing any confounding in the relationship between $D_i$ on $Y_i$, so that $(Y_i(0), \tau_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i | X_i$. (2)”

[Expression (3): p. 253 (PDF p. 4)] “We also assume that the conditional expected value of $D_i$ can be represented as a linear combination of the covariates in $X_i$. … Formally, this assumption may be written as $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = V_i\omega$, (3) where $V_i = (1 \quad X_i)$, $\omega$ is a $K + 1$ column vector of coefficients, and $\mathrm{E}[.]$ averages over the units in the population.”

[Expression (4): p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “The goal is to estimate the average causal effect for the population. This is simply the expected value of the unit-level causal effects: $\bar\tau = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_i(d') - Y_i(d)}{d' - d}\right]$, (4) where $d' \neq d$ are two arbitrary values that are possible for $D_i$.”

[Regression: section ‘Ordinary Least Squares Regression’, p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “$Y_i = \alpha + \beta D_i + X_i\gamma + \epsilon_i$, (6) where $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are model coefficients and $\epsilon_i$ is an error term. … We fit Model (6) using OLS to obtain estimates of the parameters, $\hat\alpha$, $\hat\beta$, and $\hat\gamma$. The estimate $\hat\beta$ is our regression estimate of the causal effect of $D_i$.”

[Expression (7) and the weight: p. 254 (PDF p. 5)] “$\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]}$, where $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$. (7) We call $w_i$ the multiple regression weight for unit $i$. The relation $\overset{p}{\to}$ refers to convergence in probability as the sample size, $n$, gets larger and larger”.

[Effective sample and estimated weights: section ‘The Effective Sample from Ordinary Least Squares Regression’, p. 255 (PDF p. 6)] “Expression (7) implies that the effective sample is given by reweighting the original sample by the multiple regression weights—the $w_i$s. We may estimate each of the multiple regression weights with the estimator $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$, where $\tilde D_i$ is the residual from a regression of $D_i$ on $X_i$.”

[Appendix A notation: p. 262 (PDF p. 13)] “Define $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$, a $K + 2$-length row vector combining the constant, causal factor, and control variables, and $\delta = (\alpha \quad \beta \quad \gamma)'$, a $K + 2$-length column vector containing the model coefficients. Define the stacked matrix of regressors and outcome vector as $\mathbf{W} = \begin{pmatrix} W_1 \\ \vdots \\ W_n \end{pmatrix}$ and $Y = \begin{pmatrix} Y_1 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n \end{pmatrix}$. The OLS estimates may be written as $\begin{pmatrix} \hat\alpha \\ \hat\beta \\ \hat\gamma_1 \\ \vdots \\ \hat\gamma_k \end{pmatrix} = (\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W})^{-1}\mathbf{W}'Y$. By partial regression, $\hat\beta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2}$, (12) where $\tilde D_i = D_i - V_i\hat\omega$, with $\mathbf{V} = (V_1' \quad \cdots \quad V_n')'$, $D = (D_1 \quad \cdots \quad D_n)'$, and $\hat\omega = (\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}'D$.” (The last subscript of the coefficient column is printed $k$; the dimension is $K$: finding P015-N004.) Theorem A.1 writes the baseline outcome as $Y_{0i}$, the same object as $Y_i(0)$.

[General model of the section ‘Estimating Representative Causal Effects’: p. 260 (PDF p. 11)] “we now drop the assumption of local linearity, as stated by Expression (1). We instead define causal effects over arbitrary potential outcomes: $\tau_i(d, d') = \frac{Y_i(d') - Y_i(d)}{d' - d}$, where the $d$ and $d'$ in parentheses are to emphasize that causal effects are defined for treatment values $d$ and $d'$. … we continue to assume that $X_i$ is sufficient to control for all sources confounding between $D_i$ and outcomes that would be realized under treatments $d$ or $d'$. This is expressed formally as $(Y_i(d), Y_i(d')) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|X_i$. (11) Additionally, we no longer need to assume that the conditional expectation of $D_i$ is linear in the covariates.”

[Positivity: pp. 260–261 (PDF pp. 11–12)] “Positivity, loosely speaking, requires that, for all values of $X_i$ that appear in the target population, there is some probability of observing different values of $D_i$. … Formally, the positivity assumption is as follows: $\Pr[D_i = d|X_i = x] > 0, \quad \Pr[D_i = d'|X_i = x] > 0$ for all values of $x$ in the target population represented by the nominal sample. Given unconfoundedness and positivity, the average causal effect for the target population is defined by $\bar\tau(d, d') = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i(d, d')] = \frac{\mathrm{E}[Y_i(d')] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i(d)]}{d' - d}$. Expectations ($\mathrm{E}[.]$) are taken with respect to the target population.”

[Appendix C notation: p. 265 (PDF p. 16)] “$\Pr[Y_i = 1|D_i, X_i] = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_\ell + \beta_\ell D_i + X_i\gamma_\ell)$, where $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = [1 + \exp(-a)]^{-1}$. We fit the model via maximum likelihood (ML) to obtain the coefficient vector, $\hat\theta = (\hat\alpha_\ell \quad \hat\beta_\ell \quad \hat\gamma_\ell)'$. As before, let $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$. … $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y) = \log[P_Y/(1 - P_Y)]$, where $P_Y = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$”.

[Reading used by the targets; not printed] The units $(X_i, D_i, Y_i(\cdot))$ are treated as independent draws from one distribution (the super-population reading the paper allows on p. 252), and $\mathrm{E}[.]$, $\Pr[.]$, $\mathrm{Var}[.]$ refer to that distribution. The population form of the effective sample is the reweighted law $Q(A) = \mathrm{E}[w_i\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathrm{E}[w_i]$, defined when $0 < \mathrm{E}[w_i] < \infty$; its mean of a covariate is $\mu(Z_i) = \mathrm{E}[w_iZ_i]/\mathrm{E}[w_i]$, as in Expression (9). Condition 4 of Theorem A.1 (“The data are well behaved such that the OLS solutions converge to a limit”) is read as the moment, law-of-large-numbers and nonsingularity conditions that the proof on pp. 262–263 uses (finding P015-A001, not confirmed as an error).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Random Coefficient Models’: the estimator ‘computes a series of quantities along the lines of Expression (7) and aggregates them on the basis of their precision’, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 257 (PDF p. 8), left column to right column; Expression (10) on p. 257 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed claim: p. 257 (PDF p. 8)] “Under the standard working assumption that the $\beta_g$s are independent draws from a distribution centered on $\bar\beta$, the estimator is a precision-weighted average of the group-specific OLS estimates (Hsiao and Pesaran 2008). Each of the group-specific OLS estimates is simply the value within each group of the quantity given by Expression (7). In effect, the estimator computes a series of quantities along the lines of Expression (7) and aggregates them on the basis of their precision. The precision weighting does not undo the sample distortions that the basic multiple regression weights introduce within each group. The effective sample is created from a combination of the precision weights and the within-group multiple regression weights.” Read as a statement about the treatment coefficient, this says that the pooled estimate of $\bar\beta$ is $\sum_g a_g\hat\beta_g$ for scalar precision weights $a_g$ on the within-group OLS treatment coefficients $\hat\beta_g$. [Counterexample, from the validator] Two groups of three observations, regressors $(1, D)$ with binary $D$ and no further controls, $S = I_2$ and $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = 1$: $Z_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $y_1 = (0,0,0)'$; $Z_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $y_2 = (2,2,2)'$. Then $Z_1'Z_1$ and $Z_2'Z_2$ have determinant $2$; $\hat\theta_1 = (0, 0)'$ and $\hat\theta_2 = (2, 0)'$, so both within-group OLS treatment coefficients are $0$; $P_1 = \begin{pmatrix}5/8&1/4\\1/4&1/2\end{pmatrix}$, $P_2 = \begin{pmatrix}5/7&1/7\\1/7&3/7\end{pmatrix}$; and the generalized least squares estimate is $\hat\mu = (P_1 + P_2)^{-1}(P_1\hat\theta_1 + P_2\hat\theta_2) = (68/61, \ -10/61)'$, which also equals the generalized least squares estimate computed from the raw observations, $(\sum_g Z_g'V_g^{-1}Z_g)^{-1}\sum_g Z_g'V_g^{-1}y_g$. The pooled treatment coefficient is $-10/61$, while $a_1\cdot 0 + a_2\cdot 0 = 0$ for all scalars $a_1, a_2$. For these designs and arbitrary outcomes, $\hat{\bar\beta} = \frac{5}{61}\hat\alpha_1 - \frac{5}{61}\hat\alpha_2 + \frac{32}{61}\hat\beta_1 + \frac{29}{61}\hat\beta_2$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Printed: section ‘Random Coefficient Models’, p. 257 (PDF p. 8)] “Suppose a unit $i$ is a member of one of $G$ groups indexed by $g$, where we use $g[i]$ to denote unit $i$’s group. Then the Swamy model supposes that $Y_i = \alpha_{g[i]} + \beta_{g[i]}D_i + X_i\gamma_{g[i]} + \epsilon_i$. (10) The objective is typically to estimate an average over groups (rather than units) of the group-specific coefficients; let us refer to this group-level average as $\bar\beta$. The standard estimator for the average of the group-specific coefficients is derived as the solution to a generalized least squares problem.” The paper prints no formula for the estimator. The targets use the standard Swamy (1970) form derived by the validator: for group $g$, design matrix $Z_g$ ($n_g$ rows $(1, D_i, X_i)$) with $Q_g = Z_g'Z_g$ invertible, outcomes $y_g$, group OLS vector $\hat\theta_g = Q_g^{-1}Z_g'y_g$; group coefficient vectors with common mean $\mu$ and covariance $S$, errors with variance $\sigma_g^2$; $\Omega_g = S + \sigma_g^2Q_g^{-1}$, $P_g = \Omega_g^{-1}$, $V_g = Z_gSZ_g' + \sigma_g^2I$. Expression (7) is on p. 254 (PDF p. 5).
canonical_claim.note: P015-E005 is rated an error, Minor (verdict confirmed in part). From derivation.md, section 4; exact checks in check.py and check-output.txt. The validator also shows the sample has positive probability ($19683/134217728$) under a correctly specified random-coefficient model with randomly assigned binary treatment (section 5), so the example is algebraic and is not evidence of bias or inconsistency. Not refuted: ‘precision-weighted average’ read as matrix weighting of whole coefficient vectors; footnote 17; the scalar description as a limiting approximation when within-group sample sizes grow (repeating each row $r$ times gives $(-4r-6)/(16r^2+36r+9) \to 0$); or the section's conclusion that random coefficients do not undo the within-group weighting.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Random Coefficient Models’: the description of the estimator as an aggregation of within-group Expression (7) quantities, corrected
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected text, from Sol’s smallest repair] “Let $\widehat\theta_g$ be the full vector of group-specific OLS coefficients and $P_g$ its inverse total covariance matrix. The GLS estimate is $\widehat\mu = (\sum_g P_g)^{-1}\sum_g P_g\widehat\theta_g$. Its treatment coordinate generally includes contributions from other group-specific coefficients. Expression (7) characterizes the within-group treatment OLS estimand under its assumptions and regularity conditions within that group. Pooling only these treatment quantities with prescribed scalar weights $a_g$ is valid as an exact general representation if and only if $e_\beta^{\mathsf T}(\sum_h P_h)^{-1}P_g = a_g e_\beta^{\mathsf T}$ for every group. The limiting approximation uses the treatment diagonal entries as weights: for any sequence of such models indexed by $k\in\mathbb N$ with fixed finite $G,q$ and fixed treatment coordinate $\beta$, if $(A_{g,k})_{\beta j}\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ for every $g$ and $j\ne\beta$, then $e_\beta^{\mathsf T}\sum_g A_{g,k}t_{g,k}-\sum_g (A_{g,k})_{\beta\beta}e_\beta^{\mathsf T}t_{g,k}\to0$ for every family $t_{g,k}\in\mathbb R^q$ satisfying $\sup_{k,g}\|t_{g,k}\|_\infty<\infty$. This qualification does not reject consistency under correctly specified random-coefficient and exogeneity assumptions.” [Formal content, with every hypothesis] Let $G \ge 1$ and $q \ge 1$. For each $g = 1, \ldots, G$ let $Z_g$ be an $n_g \times q$ real matrix with $Q_g = Z_g'Z_g$ invertible, $y_g \in \mathbb{R}^{n_g}$, $\hat\theta_g = Q_g^{-1}Z_g'y_g$ and $\sigma_g^2 > 0$; let $S$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $q \times q$ matrix; put $\Omega_g = S + \sigma_g^2Q_g^{-1}$ (positive definite), $P_g = \Omega_g^{-1}$, $H = \sum_g P_g$, $A_g = H^{-1}P_g$ and $V_g = Z_gSZ_g' + \sigma_g^2I_{n_g}$. (i) The unique minimizer over $m \in \mathbb{R}^q$ of $\sum_g (\hat\theta_g - m)'P_g(\hat\theta_g - m)$ is $\hat\mu = H^{-1}\sum_g P_g\hat\theta_g = \sum_g A_g\hat\theta_g$, and $\sum_g A_g = I_q$. (ii) $Z_g'V_g^{-1}Z_g = P_g$ and $Z_g'V_g^{-1}y_g = P_g\hat\theta_g$, so $\hat\mu = (\sum_g Z_g'V_g^{-1}Z_g)^{-1}\sum_g Z_g'V_g^{-1}y_g$, the generalized least squares estimator computed from the raw observations. (iii) Fix a treatment coordinate $\beta\in\{1,\ldots,q\}$, let $e_\beta \in \mathbb{R}^q$ be its coordinate vector, and fix real numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_G$. Then $e_\beta'\sum_g A_g t_g = \sum_g a_g e_\beta't_g$ for all $(t_1, \ldots, t_G) \in (\mathbb{R}^q)^G$ if and only if $e_\beta'A_g = a_g e_\beta'$ for every $g$, that is, if and only if every off-treatment entry of the treatment row of each $A_g$ is zero and $(A_g)_{\beta\beta}=a_g$ for every $g$. (iv) A sufficient case: if every $P_g$ is block diagonal between the treatment coordinate and the other coordinates, with treatment entry $p_g > 0$, then (iii) holds with $a_g = p_g/\sum_h p_h$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix C, the logistic case: the linearized estimating equations are the OLS estimating equations up to the scale factor $c$
canonical_claim.location: p. 265 (PDF p. 16), left column; main text p. 257 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: p. 265 (PDF p. 16)] “Consider the following logistic regression model: $\Pr[Y_i = 1|D_i, X_i] = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_\ell + \beta_\ell D_i + X_i\gamma_\ell)$, where $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = [1 + \exp(-a)]^{-1}$. We fit the model via maximum likelihood (ML) to obtain the coefficient vector, $\hat\theta = (\hat\alpha_\ell \quad \hat\beta_\ell \quad \hat\gamma_\ell)'$. As before, let $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$. The ML estimator for $\hat\theta$ solves the following estimating equation (Liang and Zeger 1986): $\sum_{i=1}^n \psi(Y_i, W_i, \hat\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(W_i\{Y_i - \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(W_i\hat\theta)\}\right) = \mathbf{0}_{1\times(K+2)}$, where $K$ is the number of variables in $X_i$. We may approximate the $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(.)$ function by taking a first-order Taylor expansion about $\mathrm{logit}(P_Y) = \log[P_Y/(1 - P_Y)]$, where $P_Y = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$: [display, misprinted; corrected form in P015-T13] $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) \approx \ldots = b + ca$, where $b = P_Y - P_Y(1 - P_Y)\mathrm{logit}(P_Y)$ and the scale factor $c = P_Y(1 - P_Y)$. Using the linearized $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(.)$ function, we may define approximate estimating equations: $\sum_{i=1}^n \psi(Y_i, W_i, \hat\theta) \approx \sum_{i=1}^n \tilde\psi(Y_i, W_i, \hat\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[W_i(Y_i - b - cW_i\hat\theta)\right] = \mathbf{0}_{1\times(K+2)}$. Without loss of generality, we may reframe the problem by defining an alternative coefficient vector $\tilde\theta = ((b + c\hat\alpha_\ell) \quad c\hat\beta_\ell \quad c\hat\gamma_\ell)'$, so that $\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde\psi(Y_i, W_i, \hat\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[W_i(Y_i - W_i\tilde\theta)\right] = \mathbf{0}_{1\times(K+2)}$, which are precisely the estimating equations for the OLS estimator. Thus, the only difference between the OLS estimate and the approximate logistic regression estimate of $\beta_\ell$ is the scale factor $c$. Therefore, the reweighting results for OLS hold—as a first-order approximation—for the logistic regression maximum likelihood estimator of $\beta_\ell$.” [Exact content to formalize] Let $Y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ and $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$, and let $b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ with $c \neq 0$. (i) The gradient of the logistic log likelihood $\sum_i [Y_i\log f(W_i\theta) + (1 - Y_i)\log\{1 - f(W_i\theta)\}]$, $f = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}$, is $\sum_i W_i'\{Y_i - f(W_i\theta)\}$. (ii) For $\theta = (\alpha \quad \beta \quad \gamma')'$ and $\tilde\theta = ((b + c\alpha) \quad c\beta \quad c\gamma')'$, $W_i\tilde\theta = b + cW_i\theta$ for every $i$, so $\sum_i W_i'(Y_i - b - cW_i\theta) = \sum_i W_i'(Y_i - W_i\tilde\theta)$. (iii) If $\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W}$ is invertible, the linearized equations $\sum_i W_i'(Y_i - b - cW_i\theta) = 0$ have exactly one root $\theta^* = (\alpha^* \quad \beta^* \quad \gamma^{*\prime})'$, and it satisfies $((b + c\alpha^*) \quad c\beta^* \quad c\gamma^{*\prime})' = (\mathbf{W}'\mathbf{W})^{-1}\mathbf{W}'Y$; in particular $\hat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}} = c\,\beta^*$.

(b) The decomposition (13): substituting $Y_i = Y_{0i} + \tau_iD_i$ and $D_i = \tilde D_i + V_i\hat\omega$, $\hat\beta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_iY_{0i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_iV_i\hat\omega\tau_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2\tau_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2}$. Population identities under conditions 1 and 3: (c) the display labelled (15): $\mathrm{E}[D_iY_{0i}] - \mathrm{E}[(V_i\omega)Y_{0i}] = \mathrm{E}_X[\mathrm{E}[D_iY_{0i}|X_i]] - \mathrm{E}_X[(V_i\omega)\mathrm{E}[Y_{0i}|X_i]] = \mathrm{E}_X[\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i]\mathrm{E}[Y_{0i}|X_i]] - \mathrm{E}_X[(V_i\omega)\mathrm{E}[Y_{0i}|X_i]] = 0$; (d) $\mathrm{E}[(D_i - V_i\omega)V_i\omega\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}_X[V_i\omega\,\mathrm{E}[(D_i - V_i\omega)\tau_i|X_i]] = 0$; (e) Expression (8), $\mathrm{E}[w_i|X_i] = \mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i]$ (P015-T19). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Expression (9): the weighted mean of a covariate with the estimated weights converges to its effective-sample mean
canonical_claim.location: p. 255 (PDF p. 6), right column, continued on p. 256 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: pp. 255–256 (PDF pp. 6–7)] “Expression (7) implies that the effective sample is given by reweighting the original sample by the multiple regression weights—the $w_i$s. We may estimate each of the multiple regression weights with the estimator $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$, where $\tilde D_i$ is the residual from a regression of $D_i$ on $X_i$. Then, much as we compute summary statistics for the nominal sample, we may use the multiple regression weights to estimate summary statistics for the effective sample. We can estimate the mean of a covariate $Z_i$ in the effective sample with $\hat\mu(Z_i) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \hat w_iZ_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \hat w_i} \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_iZ_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]} = \mu(Z_i)$, (9) where $\mu(.)$ refers to the mean for the effective sample.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$ (Expression (7), p. 254, PDF p. 5); $\tilde D_i = D_i - V_i\hat\omega$ with $\hat\omega = (\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}'D$ (Appendix A, p. 262, PDF p. 13); Expression (3), $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = V_i\omega$ (p. 253, PDF p. 4). $Z_i$ is a real covariate measured on unit $i$ (the paper's example, p. 256: an indicator for ‘unit is in Europe’). The paper states no regularity conditions for (9) and gives no proof; a sufficient reading, in the manner of condition 4 of Theorem A.1: independent draws from one distribution, Expression (3), $\mathrm{E}[V_i'V_i]$ nonsingular, $0 < \mathrm{E}[w_i] < \infty$, and convergence in probability to finite expectations of the sample averages of $V_i'V_i$, $V_i'D_i$, $w_iZ_i$, $w_i$, $(D_i - V_i\omega)Z_iV_i$, $(D_i - V_i\omega)V_i$, $Z_iV_i'V_i$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Not printed (the paper gives no proof of (9)); the exact identity on which the limit rests, for each $n$: since $\tilde D_i = (D_i - V_i\omega) - V_i(\hat\omega - \omega)$, $\frac1n\sum_i \hat w_iZ_i = \frac1n\sum_i w_iZ_i - 2\left[\frac1n\sum_i (D_i - V_i\omega)Z_iV_i\right](\hat\omega - \omega) + (\hat\omega - \omega)'\left[\frac1n\sum_i Z_iV_i'V_i\right](\hat\omega - \omega)$, and the same with $Z_i \equiv 1$ for the denominator. Also exact, on both of the paper's data sets and in general: $\sum_i \tilde D_iY_i/\sum_i \hat w_i = \hat\beta$ (Expression (12)).
canonical_claim.note: The formal part of headline claim P015-H2 (the effective sample can be studied by reweighting with the squared residuals). Both readers checked that (9) follows from $\hat\omega \overset{p}{\to} \omega$ and a law of large numbers; the formula held up. The reader's ‘problem found’ under this claim is the country-level implementation in the Jensen example (means in place of sums, P015-E001, Moderate), which is a finding about computed numbers with no mathematical statement to correct and is not a target. The regularity conditions in definitions_needed are this brief's sufficient reading and should appear as explicit hypotheses.

canonical_claim.location: p. 263 (PDF p. 14); main-text form in section ‘Randomized Experiments’, p. 256 (PDF p. 7)
canonical_claim.statement: Corollary A.1. Given the data-generating process outlined in the main text, if $D_i$ is randomly assigned, then as $n \to \infty$, $\hat\beta \overset{p}{\to} \bar\tau$. Proof. Under random assignment, $w_i \perp \tau_i$. Then, by random sampling and Slutsky’s theorem, $\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2\tau_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde D_i^2} \overset{p}{\to} \frac{\mathrm{E}[w_i]\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]}{\mathrm{E}[w_i]} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \bar\tau$. □ [The hypothesis ‘randomly assigned’ as the main text states it: section ‘Randomized Experiments’, p. 256 (PDF p. 7)] “suppose that $D_i$ were randomly assigned, as would be the case in a well-executed randomized experiment with equal assignment probabilities. Then $D_i$ would be independent of $\tau_i$ as well as $X_i$, in which case $w_i$ would be independent of $\tau_i$. As a result, the weights in Expression (7) would effectively cancel out, and $\hat\beta$ would converge to $\bar\tau$. (See Corollary A.1 in the appendix.)”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for Theorem A.1 (P015-T22): Expressions (1), (4), (6), (7), $\tilde D_i$, and the reading of condition 4. ‘Randomly assigned’ is read, as on p. 256, as $D_i$ independent of $(Y_i(0), \tau_i, X_i)$ with one assignment distribution for all units (equal assignment probabilities); then Expression (2) holds, and Expression (3) holds with $\omega = (\mathrm{E}[D_i], 0, \ldots, 0)'$. Footnote 15 (p. 256, PDF p. 7) excludes designs with assignment probabilities that vary across units: for those the regression “will estimate a reweighted causal effect as in Expression (7)”.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact population facts on which the limit rests: if $D_i$ is independent of $(\tau_i, X_i)$ then $\mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i] = \mathrm{E}[D_i]$, so $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i])^2$ is a function of $D_i$ alone, hence independent of $\tau_i$, and $\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}[w_i]\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$; with $\mathrm{E}[w_i] = \mathrm{Var}[D_i] > 0$, $\mathrm{E}[w_i\tau_i]/\mathrm{E}[w_i] = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \bar\tau$. The rest is Theorem A.1 (P015-T22) and its finite lemmas. For contrast (batch validator; consistent with footnote 15): with $\Pr[X=0] = \Pr[X=1] = 1/2$, $\Pr[D=1|X=0] = 4/5$, $\Pr[D=1|X=1] = 1/10$, $\tau = 0$ at $X = 0$ and $\tau = 2$ at $X = 1$, $\bar\tau = 1$ while $\mathrm{E}[w\tau]/\mathrm{E}[w] = 18/25$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P015-H3. Both readers found the corollary and its proof correct given $D_i$ independent of $(Y_i(0), \tau_i, X_i)$, the equal-probability experiment of the main text. The allegation that the corollary omits the equal-probability condition (P015-A002) was not confirmed: the statement imports the main-text data-generating process, and footnote 15 covers unequal probabilities; so related_finding is null. The printed proof writes $w_i \perp \tau_i$ with a single perpendicular sign for independence. State the limit as convergence in probability under the hypotheses of Theorem A.1 together with the independence reading above, and prove the finite lemma.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix C (opening paragraph, estimating equation and closing sentences) and pp. 256–257: the extension of the OLS weighting result to nonlinear models fit by maximum likelihood
canonical_claim.location: pp. 264–265 (PDF pp. 15–16); main text pp. 256–257 (PDF pp. 7–8)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: Appendix C, pp. 264–265 (PDF pp. 15–16)] “We illustrate the case of implicit weighting for a logistic regression with treatment, $D_i$, and a vector of control variables, $X_i$. The illustration relies on a first-order approximation of the inverse link function for logistic regression. The approximation is necessary because there is no closed-form solution to the coefficient vector from a logistic regression. While our illustration is for logistic regression, the results hold for any nonlinear model that can be expressed in terms of estimating equations in the manner that follows (Liang and Zeger 1986). This holds for generalized linear models such as probit, Poisson regression, ordered logit or probit, multinomial logit or probit, and duration models (McCullagh and Nelder 1999). To apply the result below for these other models, one substitutes the relevant predicted mean or inverse link function into the estimating equation.” The estimating equation (p. 265): “The ML estimator for $\hat\theta$ solves the following estimating equation (Liang and Zeger 1986): $\sum_{i=1}^n \psi(Y_i, W_i, \hat\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(W_i\{Y_i - \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(W_i\hat\theta)\}\right) = \mathbf{0}_{1\times(K+2)}$, where $K$ is the number of variables in $X_i$.” The closing sentences (p. 265): “Therefore, the reweighting results for OLS hold—as a first-order approximation—for the logistic regression maximum likelihood estimator of $\beta_\ell$. As mentioned above, analogous results can be derived for the maximum likelihood estimators of the coefficients in other generalized linear models.” [Printed: main text, pp. 256–257 (PDF pp. 7–8)] “We show that these estimators apply the same multiple regression weights that OLS does, either exactly or approximately.” “The results for linear regression carry over directly to nonlinear regression models fit via maximum likelihood. This includes the class of generalized linear models, such as logit, probit, multinomial logit or probit, Poisson regression, and parametric or semiparametric (e.g., Cox) duration models (Long 1997; McCullagh and Nelder 1999).” “Suppose we center such an expansion on the logit of the mean of $Y_i$. Then, to a first approximation, the only difference between $\hat\beta_\ell$ and what we would get were we to just use OLS on these data is a scaling factor that depends solely on the mean of $Y_i$. Therefore, the weights implied by a logistic regression are approximately equal to the multiple regression weights from OLS. … (See Appendix C for the mathematical details. The logic extends to maximum likelihood estimates of any generalized linear model.)” [The mathematical claims in these passages] (A) For logistic regression the maximum likelihood estimator solves the displayed residual estimating equation. (B) For each of the other listed models, the maximum likelihood estimating equation is obtained from (A) by substituting that model's predicted mean or inverse link function. (C) Consequently, to a first-order approximation, the maximum likelihood estimate of the treatment coefficient in any generalized linear model differs from the OLS estimate only by a scale factor that depends solely on the mean of $Y_i$, so that the OLS weights carry over.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $W_i = (1 \quad D_i \quad X_i)$, $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(a) = [1 + \exp(-a)]^{-1}$, $\hat\theta = (\hat\alpha_\ell \quad \hat\beta_\ell \quad \hat\gamma_\ell)'$, $P_Y = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$ (Appendix C, p. 265, PDF p. 16; transcribed in the standing assumptions). The paper writes the estimating equation with the row vector $W_i$; the targets write the same equation as a column, $\sum_i W_i'\{Y_i - m(W_i\theta)\} = 0$. For a Bernoulli outcome with mean function (inverse link) $m$, the log likelihood is $\ell(\theta) = \sum_i [Y_i\log m(W_i\theta) + (1 - Y_i)\log\{1 - m(W_i\theta)\}]$, and an ML estimate is a maximizer of $\ell$; these standard definitions are not printed in the paper. $\Phi$ and $\phi$ are the standard normal distribution function and density.
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, listed because P015-E008 is rated Moderate. (A) is true (P015-T8 (ii)). (B) is false: exact counterexamples P015-T5 (a rational Bernoulli link) and P015-T6 (probit). (C) is not established by the argument and fails at first order in exact examples (P015-T7); it holds for logit and, by the same argument, for canonical-link models such as Poisson with log link (P015-T8 (ii), P015-T21). The itemization (A)–(C) is this brief's reading of the passages, following both validators. Ordered, multinomial and duration models were not audited individually. The corrected statement is P015-T8.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section ‘Estimating Representative Causal Effects’: the paragraph connecting positivity and the multiple regression weights
canonical_claim.location: p. 261 (PDF p. 12), last paragraph of the left column to the right column; positivity display on p. 261 (PDF p. 12)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed: p. 261 (PDF p. 12), last paragraph of the left column to the right column] “We can draw a connection between the positivity assumption and the results that we obtained above for multiple regression. The positivity assumption implies that $\mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i = x] > 0$, for all values of $x$. Thus, when a multiple regression places (either approximately or exactly) no weight on a set of units with a given covariate profile, this result implies that positivity is violated and representative causal effects cannot be estimated for the target population without assumption-based extrapolation or interpolation. Examination of the effective sample provides insight about what can be learned from any given study. In the Jensen (2003) study, many substantively important countries—including Russia and China—cannot be included in estimates of the causal effects of regime type on FDI. No consistent, extrapolation-free estimator of $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i(d, d')]$ is available for any $(d, d')$ if our interest is in the average over the entirety of the 114 countries in the nominal sample. This is not due to any fault on Jensen’s part; it is an implication of the variation that nature has provided. However, in other studies, such as Gerber and Huber (2010), positivity appears to hold, and thus estimation of representative average causal effects is straightforward. Of course, the effective sample that multiple regression generates is one for which positivity holds by construction. In conjunction with the linearity assumptions embodied by Expressions (1) and (3) (assumptions that are with little loss of generality when $D_i$ is binary), regression facilitates estimation in a manner that reflects the regions of the data where causal inference is possible.” [The three mathematical implications in the passage] (A) Positivity for $(d, d')$, $d \neq d'$, at every $x$ implies $\mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i = x] > 0$ for every $x$. (B) If the regression places approximately or exactly no weight on the units with covariate profile $x$, then positivity is violated, and no consistent estimator of $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i(d, d')]$ for the target population exists without extrapolation or interpolation. (C) In the effective sample, positivity holds.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_i = (D_i - \mathrm{E}[D_i|X_i])^2$ (Expression (7), p. 254, PDF p. 5); $\mathrm{E}[w_i|X_i] = \mathrm{Var}[D_i|X_i]$ (Expression (8), p. 255, PDF p. 6); the effective sample as the reweighting of the sample by the $w_i$ and the estimated weights $\hat w_i = \tilde D_i^2$ (p. 255, PDF p. 6); $\tau_i(d, d')$, unconfoundedness (11), the positivity display and $\bar\tau(d, d')$ (pp. 260–261, PDF pp. 11–12); all transcribed in the standing assumptions. Formal reading: ‘the weight a multiple regression places on the units with covariate profile $x$’ is the effective-population mass $Q(X = x) = \Pr[X = x]\,\mathrm{Var}[D|X = x]/\mathrm{E}[w]$, with $Q(A) = \mathrm{E}[w\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathrm{E}[w]$; in a sample it is the share $\sum_{i: X_i = x}\hat w_i/\sum_i \hat w_i$. ‘Positivity for $(d, d')$’ is the printed display at every $x$ with $\Pr[X = x] > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, listed because P015-E006 is rated Moderate. (A) is true (P015-T4 (i)). (B) is false for approximately zero weight (P015-T1) and for exactly zero estimated weight (P015-T3); it is true for exactly zero population weight (P015-T4 (i)). (C) is false for the formal pair-specific display with a multivalued treatment (P015-T2) and true for a binary treatment (P015-T4 (iii)). The itemization (A)–(C) is this brief's reading of the passage, agreed by both validators; the sentences about Jensen (2003) and Gerber and Huber (2010) are applied conclusions drawn from (B) and (C) and are not themselves formal statements. The corrected statement is P015-T4.
